datasheet-001.question: Which correctly describes the difference between "absolute maximum ratings" and "recommended operating conditions" in a datasheet?
choices: Within the absolute maximum ratings the device will not be damaged, and all values in the electrical characteristics table are also guaranteed as written
Absolute maximum ratings are limits beyond which damage may occur; characteristics are guaranteed only within the recommended operating conditions
Recommended operating conditions are the limits for continuous operation, while absolute maximum ratings are limits that may be used routinely for short periods
datasheet-001.explanation: Absolute maximum ratings are limit values that, if exceeded even momentarily, may cause damage or degradation; staying within them only means the device will not be damaged—it does not guarantee correct operation. The values in the electrical characteristics table are guaranteed only within the recommended operating conditions. For example, a 3.3 V device might specify an absolute maximum supply voltage of −0.3 to 4.6 V and recommended operating conditions of 3.0 to 3.6 V. In design, use the device within the recommended operating conditions, and confirm that the absolute maximum ratings are not exceeded even including noise and surges.

datasheet-002.question: On a prototype board, a surge was found that momentarily pushes the supply voltage above its absolute maximum rating. The IC still works normally afterward. Which is the appropriate way to think about this?
choices: The IC may have degraded internally and its reliability is no longer guaranteed, so fix the surge, replace the IC and re-evaluate
Since it works normally, it can be judged undamaged, and you can proceed to mass production without any particular countermeasure
Absolute maximum ratings apply to continuously applied values, so exceeding them for a very short time is not a particular problem
datasheet-002.explanation: Absolute maximum ratings must not be exceeded even momentarily, regardless of duration. Even if the device works right after the event, the gate oxide, junctions or protection elements may be partially damaged, and failures can appear later as increased leakage current or shortened lifetime. Parts that have been overstressed should therefore be treated as outside the reliability guarantee and replaced, and the evaluation repeated after suppressing the surge with TVS diodes, filters or the like. Datasheets typically include a note such as "Stresses beyond those listed may cause permanent damage to the device."

datasheet-003.question: Which correctly describes the concept of component "derating"?
choices: Ratings already include margin, so using parts right up to their ratings is the most economical
Run parts briefly under conditions harsher than their ratings and use only those that pass
To improve reliability, use parts with margin on voltage, temperature and so on rather than right up to their ratings
datasheet-003.explanation: Derating is the design practice of using parts with margin relative to their ratings. Companies and industries set guidelines such as keeping voltage at or below 70–80% of the rating and junction temperature at or below 125 °C against a 150 °C maximum rating. Component failure rates rise with greater temperature and voltage stress, so more margin means longer life. Running parts under conditions harsher than their ratings to weed out early failures is screening (burn-in), a technique separate from derating.

datasheet-004.question: Which correctly describes "typ (typical)" in an electrical characteristics table?
choices: The most reliable value in the table, measured and verified on every unit in pre-shipment testing
A guide to the representative value when many units are measured; it is not guaranteed for individual units
A value for design use, calculated as the average of the minimum (min) and maximum (max)
datasheet-004.explanation: The typ value is a guide to the representative value near the center of the characteristic's spread, usually at 25 °C and nominal supply voltage. Individual units are not guaranteed to have this value. What the manufacturer guarantees are the min/max values, which are backed by production testing and characterization. The typ is not necessarily midway between min and max, and parameters given only as typ should be treated as reference values. Design calculations should basically use min or max, depending on the conditions.

datasheet-005.question: A load switch (an IC that turns a power rail on and off) has a current limit specified as min 1.0 A, typ 1.5 A, max 2.2 A. You want to draw up to 1.2 A for the load. Which judgment is correct?
choices: The typ value is 1.5 A, so there is 0.3 A of margin and it can be drawn without problems
It is about half the max value of 2.2 A, so it can be drawn without problems with ample margin
Some units may enter current limit near 1.0 A, so there is no guarantee that 1.2 A can be drawn
datasheet-005.explanation: The current limit varies from unit to unit over 1.0–2.2 A; with a unit near 1.0 A, current limiting kicks in as soon as you try to draw 1.2 A, and the output voltage drops. To be sure the required current can always be drawn, choose a part whose minimum current limit (1.0 A) is greater than the load current. Conversely, use the max value of 2.2 A when estimating the current that can flow under fault conditions. Judging by the typ value leads to problems where the prototype works but some units fail in mass production.

datasheet-006.question: The top of an electrical characteristics table states "Ta = 25 °C, VDD = 3.3 V unless otherwise noted." Which is a correct point to note when reading this table?
choices: Values can change with temperature and supply voltage, so also check the values and graphs specified over the full temperature range
This condition merely records the test equipment settings and need not be of particular concern in design
The 25 °C values are the worst case, so values at other temperatures will be better than these
datasheet-006.explanation: Electrical characteristic values are meaningful only together with their test conditions, such as temperature, supply voltage and load. The conditions at the top apply to every parameter whose row does not state other conditions. Values can change greatly with conditions: leakage current increases at high temperature, and output drive capability decreases at low supply voltage, for example. Many datasheets show values guaranteed over the full temperature range, such as −40 to 85 °C, in a separate column or in bold, so read the rows that match the actual operating conditions.

datasheet-007.question: In an electrical characteristics table, what does a footnote saying "Guaranteed by design and characterization; not production tested" mean for that parameter?
choices: Not every unit is measured, but the manufacturer guarantees the value based on design and characterization data
The value is shown for reference only, and the manufacturer guarantees nothing about it
The value is measured on every unit before shipment and is the most tightly controlled in the table
datasheet-007.explanation: In production testing, not every parameter is measured on every unit, owing to test time and cost. Parameters that are hard to measure, such as input capacitance and some timing parameters, are guaranteed by design analysis and by characterization data taken while varying temperature and supply voltage. A min/max value with this note can still be treated as guaranteed, but since it is not based on 100% testing, it is safer to use it with margin. Read it as distinct from typ values, which are not guaranteed.

datasheet-008.question: A voltage of 1.4 V is applied to an input of an IC whose input thresholds are specified as VIH(min) = 2.0 V and VIL(max) = 0.8 V. How is it interpreted?
choices: It is below VIH(min) of 2.0 V, so it is always interpreted as L
It is above VIL(max) of 0.8 V, so it is always interpreted as H
Whether it is interpreted as H or L is not guaranteed
datasheet-008.explanation: VIH(min) is the lowest voltage guaranteed to be recognized as H, and VIL(max) is the highest voltage guaranteed to be recognized as L. The range between them, 0.8–2.0 V, is an undefined region where the input may be recognized either way depending on the unit and temperature. If an input stays in this region for long, the output may oscillate, or the pMOS and nMOS of the input stage may turn on simultaneously and shoot-through current may flow. For slowly changing signals, use a Schmitt-trigger input with hysteresis.

datasheet-009.question: The driving IC has VOH(min) = 2.9 V and VOL(max) = 0.4 V, and the receiving IC has VIH(min) = 2.0 V and VIL(max) = 0.8 V. What is the low-level noise margin?
datasheet-009.explanation: The low-level noise margin is VIL(max) − VOL(max) = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V. The output drives an L of 0.4 V or less even in the worst case, and the input recognizes up to 0.8 V as L, so noise up to the 0.4 V difference will not cause a misread. The high-level noise margin is VOH(min) − VIH(min) = 2.9 − 2.0 = 0.9 V. Noise margin is thus found by combining the guaranteed values of the driver and receiver, and the smaller one is the weak point of that connection. 0.8 V is VIL(max) itself.

datasheet-010.question: Which correctly describes the problem with connecting the output of an IC powered from 3.3 V directly to a CMOS input powered from 5 V (VIH(min) = 0.7 × VDD)?
choices: VIH(min) becomes 3.5 V, so a 3.3 V high level cannot be reliably recognized as H
A 3.3 V signal is an overvoltage for the 5 V side's input, so the input pin will be damaged
The high level exceeds 2.5 V, half the supply voltage, so they can be connected without problems
datasheet-010.explanation: For a 5 V CMOS input with VIH(min) = 0.7 × VDD, VIH(min) is 3.5 V. The high level of the 3.3 V side's output is at most about 3.3 V, so it does not reach VIH(min) and is not guaranteed to be recognized as H. Remedies include using an IC with TTL-compatible inputs, whose VIH(min) is 2.0 V, or inserting a level-shifter IC. Applying a signal lower than the supply voltage does not in itself damage the input; the problem is that the logic levels do not match.

datasheet-011.question: What does it mean when a datasheet describes an input pin as "5 V tolerant"?
choices: The device is guaranteed to operate with the same performance whether the supply voltage is 5 V or 3.3 V
The pin can output a 5 V high-level signal
Even when the device runs from a supply such as 3.3 V, a 5 V signal may be applied to that input
datasheet-011.explanation: A normal CMOS input has an ESD protection diode to the supply (VDD), and if the input exceeds about VDD + 0.3 V, the diode conducts and current flows in. A 5 V tolerant input is designed without this path, so applying 5 V while the supply is 3.3 V causes neither damage nor current inflow. It only tolerates the input; it does not mean the output reaches 5 V. Whether 5 V may also be applied while the supply is off must be checked in a separate statement.

datasheet-012.question: Which correctly describes the change when the value of the pull-up resistor on an open-drain output is reduced?
choices: The rise becomes slower, but the current flowing while the output is low decreases, reducing power consumption
The rise becomes faster, but the current flowing while the output is low increases, and VOL also tends to rise
The high-level voltage rises above the pull-up supply voltage, making it easier to exceed the receiver's input rating
datasheet-012.explanation: The high level of an open-drain output is produced by the pull-up resistor pulling the signal line up while the output transistor is off. The rise speed is set by the time constant of the resistor and the line capacitance—for example, 1 µs for 10 kΩ and 100 pF. A smaller resistor makes it faster, but when the output is low, current flows from the supply through the resistor: 3.3 mA for 3.3 V and 1 kΩ. If this current exceeds the IOL condition in the datasheet, VOL will not stay within its specified value, so choose a value that satisfies both.

datasheet-013.question: What is the main problem when many CMOS inputs are connected to a single output of a CMOS logic IC?
choices: The total DC current into the inputs reaches the mA range, and the output can no longer hold the high level
The output's high-level voltage rises above the supply voltage in proportion to the number of connected inputs
The total input capacitance becomes large, slowing the signal's rise and fall and increasing the propagation delay
datasheet-013.explanation: The number of inputs connected to one output is called the fan-out. The DC input current of a CMOS input is small—a few µA or less even at max—so considering DC current alone, fan-out is hardly limited. In practice, each input adds a few pF of input capacitance in parallel, so the more inputs there are, the longer charging and discharging take and the greater the delay. Datasheet propagation delays are specified under load capacitance conditions such as CL = 15 pF or 50 pF, so read them against the total capacitance including wiring.

datasheet-014.question: A microcontroller's operating current is specified as "120 µA/MHz." When it runs at 16 MHz, roughly what is its operating current?
choices: About 1.9 mA
About 7.5 µA
About 19 mA
datasheet-014.explanation: The µA/MHz notation indicates that operating current is roughly proportional to clock frequency. 120 µA × 16 = 1920 µA, or about 1.9 mA. This is because dynamic power in CMOS circuits is proportional to the capacitance being charged and discharged, the square of the supply voltage and the frequency. However, this value is typically measured under specific conditions, such as running a particular program with peripherals stopped, so add the current of the peripherals in use and leakage current separately in the estimate. About 7.5 µA is the mistake of dividing 120 by 16.

datasheet-015.question: What is the main reason standby current is specified per temperature, such as "typ 0.5 µA at 25 °C, max 10 µA at 85 °C"?
choices: Because wiring resistance increases with temperature, causing correspondingly more current to flow
Because transistor leakage current increases sharply as temperature rises
Because the internal clock frequency automatically increases at high temperature
datasheet-015.explanation: In standby the clock is stopped, and most of the current consumption is transistor subthreshold leakage and junction leakage. These increase exponentially with temperature, and it is not unusual for them to grow several to several tens of times from 25 °C to 85 °C. For battery-powered equipment, battery life must be estimated using the value at the upper end of the operating temperature range. Increased wiring resistance would, if anything, reduce current, so it is not the reason.

datasheet-016.question: Which correctly describes the "quiescent current (IQ)" of a linear regulator?
choices: Leakage current that flows backward from the output pin toward the input pin when the output is turned off
The maximum output current, guaranteed in the datasheet, that the regulator can supply to the load
Current that flows to ground for the regulator's own operation, separate from the current flowing to the load
datasheet-016.explanation: Quiescent current is the current consumed by the regulator's internal circuits, such as the voltage reference and error amplifier, so that input current = load current + quiescent current. It ranges from under 1 µA to several mA depending on the product. For example, using a regulator with 50 µA quiescent current in equipment whose standby load current is 10 µA means most of the battery drain goes to the regulator itself. In some products the quiescent current increases with load current, so check the values and graphs at no load and under load.

datasheet-017.question: What is the main reason a datasheet for an IC with two supplies—1.0 V for the core and 3.3 V for I/O—specifies a power-up sequence?
choices: Because the power-up order determines the upper limit of the maximum operating frequency at which the product can run stably
Because the wrong order can cause unintended internal current, leading to latch-up, damage or malfunction
Because the order affects only power consumption at startup and has no effect on function or reliability
datasheet-017.explanation: In an IC with multiple supplies, when only one supply is on, unexpected current can flow between supplies or through protection diodes on I/O pins. This can cause latch-up, device damage or malfunction due to undefined internal states. Datasheets give conditions such as "apply the core supply first and remove supplies in reverse order" or "keep the voltage difference between supplies below a certain value." On actual boards, the sequence is created using regulator enable pins and power-good signals.

datasheet-018.question: Which correctly describes what can happen when a 3.3 V signal from another circuit is applied to an input pin of an IC that is not powered?
choices: Current flows into the supply rail through the input protection diode, which can lead to malfunction or pin damage
With no power applied, the input pin is the same as an open circuit, so nothing in particular happens
Power supplied through the input pin causes the entire IC to start up properly and begin operating normally
datasheet-018.explanation: In many CMOS ICs, the absolute maximum rating of an input pin is defined relative to the supply voltage, as in "−0.3 V to VDD + 0.3 V." If 3.3 V is applied while the supply is at 0 V, the protection diode from the input to VDD conducts, and current flows from the signal line into the supply rail (back-powering). As a result, the supply rail may be pulled up to an intermediate voltage, causing malfunction, or the input clamp current rating may be exceeded, damaging the pin. Some products have protection that permits inputs while powered off, so check the datasheet.

datasheet-019.question: What is the main reason a datasheet recommends "placing a 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor as close as possible to each supply pin"?
choices: To lower the DC resistance of the supply line and thereby reduce the IC's average current consumption
Because longer wiring reduces the capacitance of the capacitor itself accordingly
To reduce wiring inductance and suppress supply voltage fluctuations caused by rapid current changes
datasheet-019.explanation: Digital circuits draw large currents from the supply for short periods on every clock. The wiring from the supply to the IC has inductance L, which produces a voltage drop of L × di/dt in response to current changes. For example, with 2 nH of wiring and a current change of 0.1 A/ns, the supply voltage drops by as much as 0.2 V. Placing the capacitor right next to the pin lets it supply this current over a short path. Wiring length does not change the capacitance value itself; the problem is the inductance of the path.

datasheet-020.question: The transmitting IC has a clock-to-output delay of max 6 ns, the board trace delay is 1 ns, and the receiving IC has a setup time of 3 ns. Ignoring clock skew, what is the maximum usable clock frequency?
choices: 100 MHz
About 143 MHz
250 MHz
datasheet-020.explanation: The slowest time for data to reach the receiver is 6 + 1 = 7 ns. At the receiver, the data must be valid 3 ns before the next clock edge, so the clock period must be at least 7 + 3 = 10 ns, giving a maximum frequency of 1/10 ns = 100 MHz. The key point in checking setup is to use the maximum (max) delay. About 143 MHz is the value obtained by forgetting to add the setup time (1/7 ns). In real designs, margin for clock skew and jitter is also subtracted.

datasheet-021.question: When checking whether the receiver's hold time is met, which value of the transmitter's clock-to-output delay should be used?
choices: Minimum (min)
Maximum (max)
Typical (typ)
datasheet-021.explanation: Hold time is the time data must continue to be held after the clock edge. When the transmitter outputs the next data on the same clock edge, the previous data at the receiver is replaced earliest when the delay is shortest. Therefore, check that the sum of the min clock-to-output delay and the minimum trace delay is at least the hold time. If the datasheet gives no min value, estimate on the safe side, for example by assuming 0 ns. The max value is used for setup checks.

datasheet-022.question: Which is the common definition of the propagation delay tPLH in a logic IC datasheet?
choices: The time it takes for the output to go from 10% to 90% of its swing when changing from L to H
The time from the input changing from L to H until the output reaches the fully settled 100% point
The time from an input change until the output changes from L to H, measured between the 50% points of the swings
datasheet-022.explanation: tPLH is the propagation delay when the output changes from L to H, and tPHL is the delay when it changes from H to L; the two are generally not equal. The reference points are usually 50% (VDD/2) of the input and output swings respectively, though 1.5 V is sometimes used for TTL families. The time to go from 10% to 90% of the swing is the rise time, a separate parameter from propagation delay. Delay varies with load capacitance, supply voltage and temperature, so read it together with the test conditions in the table.

datasheet-023.question: What is the main reason a logic IC's recommended operating conditions specify an upper limit on how slow input rise and fall can be (for example, 10 ns/V)?
choices: Because a slow input change overcharges the capacitance of the input pin, damaging the input pin
Because an input lingering near the threshold increases shoot-through current or causes the output to oscillate
Because the slower the input change, the shorter the propagation delay becomes, causing malfunction in later stages
datasheet-023.explanation: A slowly changing input lingers at intermediate voltages where H/L recognition is undefined. During that time, the pMOS and nMOS of the input stage are both partially on, and shoot-through current flows from the supply to ground, increasing current consumption and heat. Noise can also make the decision flip H, L, H repeatedly, causing the output to oscillate. For this reason, the recommended operating conditions set a lower limit on input transition speed. When slow signals must be received, choose a product with Schmitt-trigger inputs that have hysteresis.

datasheet-024.question: In a timing diagram, what is meant by the notation in which an address or data bus is drawn as two parallel lines, upper and lower, that cross in an × shape here and there?
choices: Sections with parallel lines indicate that the signal is oscillating rapidly between H and L
Sections with parallel lines indicate that the value is valid, and the value changes at each ×
Each × indicates that the output goes into a high-impedance (open) state at that moment
datasheet-024.explanation: In a multi-bit bus, whether each bit is H or L depends on the data, so both the H and L lines are drawn in parallel to show a section where "some value is valid." The × crossing marks the point where that value changes, and setup and hold times are shown as the interval between this transition and the clock edge. High impedance is generally drawn as a single line at mid-height, and sections where the value is invalid are drawn with hatching. Check the legend in the datasheet for notation conventions.

datasheet-025.question: Which is a correct caution when using the θJA (junction-to-ambient thermal resistance) given in a datasheet for the thermal design of real equipment?
choices: It is determined solely by the package structure, so the value does not change regardless of the board it is mounted on
The larger the copper area on the board, the more heat is trapped, so θJA increases
It is measured on a test board, so it varies greatly with the actual board's copper area, number of layers and airflow
datasheet-025.explanation: θJA is measured with the IC mounted on a test board defined by standards such as JEDEC, inside an enclosure with still air. Much of the heat flows from the package through the pins and the exposed pad on the bottom into the board, so θJA depends strongly on the board. Even for the same package, it can differ by nearly a factor of two between a small single-layer board and a multilayer board with many solid planes. Enlarging the copper area or adding airflow makes θJA smaller (easier heat dissipation). Treat the datasheet value as a guide for comparison, and verify by measuring temperature on the actual equipment.

datasheet-026.question: An IC with maximum junction temperature Tj(max) = 125 °C and θJA = 50 °C/W is used at an ambient temperature Ta = 85 °C. What is the upper limit on allowable power dissipation?
datasheet-026.explanation: Junction temperature is given by Tj = Ta + P × θJA. Solving for P gives P = (Tj(max) − Ta)/θJA = (125 − 85)/50 = 0.8 W. The higher the ambient temperature, the smaller the allowable temperature rise, and so the smaller the allowable power. 2.5 W is the mistake of forgetting to subtract the ambient temperature (125/50), and 1.7 W is the mistake of computing 85/50. In practice, considering that θJA varies with the board and allowing derating margin, design to keep power below the calculated value.

datasheet-027.question: When estimating the junction temperature of a power device used with a heatsink, which combination should be used as the junction-to-ambient thermal resistance?
choices: The datasheet θJA (junction-to-ambient) plus the heatsink-to-ambient thermal resistance
The sum of θJC, the case-to-heatsink contact thermal resistance and the heatsink-to-ambient thermal resistance
Only the datasheet θJA (junction-to-ambient); attaching a heatsink does not change the value
datasheet-027.explanation: θJC is the thermal resistance from the junction to the package's heat-dissipating surface (the case), measured with the case held at a constant temperature. With a heatsink attached, most heat flows from the case into the heatsink, so θJC, the contact thermal resistance θCS of thermal grease or similar, and the heatsink thermal resistance θSA are added in series. For example, 1.0 + 0.5 + 3.0 = 4.5 °C/W, so a 10 W loss gives a temperature rise of 45 °C. θJA is measured without a heatsink, with the device mounted on a test board, so it cannot be used in this case.

datasheet-028.question: Which is the correct use of the ψJT (junction-to-top-of-package thermal characterization parameter) given in a datasheet?
choices: Add power dissipation × ψJT to the ambient temperature to find junction temperature in place of θJA
Use it as the thermal resistance when a heatsink is attached to the top of the package, for selecting a heatsink
Measure the package top temperature on the actual equipment and add power dissipation × ψJT to estimate junction temperature
datasheet-028.explanation: ψJT is the difference between junction temperature and top-surface temperature divided by power dissipation, under normal mounting conditions where almost all heat flows somewhere other than the package top (mainly into the board). Because it is not a thermal resistance representing a heat-flow path, it is denoted ψ rather than θ. If the top temperature Tt is measured on the actual equipment with a thermocouple or similar, junction temperature can be estimated as Tj ≈ Tt + P × ψJT. For example, with Tt = 70 °C, P = 1 W and ψJT = 2 °C/W, Tj is about 72 °C. ψJT is a small value, so calculating from the ambient temperature greatly underestimates junction temperature.

datasheet-029.question: A package's allowable power dissipation is 1.0 W up to an ambient temperature of 25 °C, and above that it decreases linearly to 0 W at 150 °C. What is the allowable power dissipation at an ambient temperature of 75 °C?
datasheet-029.explanation: It decreases by 1.0 W over the 125 °C span from 25 °C to 150 °C, so the slope is 1.0 W ÷ 125 °C = 8 mW/°C. 75 °C is 50 °C above 25 °C, so the reduction is 50 × 8 mW = 0.4 W, and the allowable dissipation is 1.0 − 0.4 = 0.6 W. 0.4 W is the reduction itself, and 0.5 W is the mistake of a proportional calculation starting from 0 °C. This curve is determined by the maximum junction temperature of 150 °C and θJA (here 125 °C/W); note also that, like θJA, it is a value for a test board.

datasheet-030.question: A silicon power MOSFET's datasheet gives RDS(on) = 10 mΩ (Tj = 25 °C, VGS = 10 V). Which is the correct approach when using it at around Tj = 125 °C?
choices: Semiconductor resistance falls as temperature rises, so estimating with the 25 °C value errs on the safe side
RDS(on) increases at higher temperature, so correct it to the high-temperature value using the temperature characteristic graph and estimate the loss
RDS(on) hardly depends on temperature, so the table value can be used as is to calculate conduction loss
datasheet-030.explanation: The RDS(on) of a silicon power MOSFET increases with temperature because carrier mobility decreases; at 125 °C it is typically about 1.5 to 2 times the 25 °C value. Datasheets include a graph of normalized RDS(on) versus temperature, with the 25 °C value as 1. Calculating conduction loss I²R with the 25 °C value underestimates the loss and overlooks the vicious circle in which heating raises the resistance further. This positive temperature coefficient also has the advantage of tending to equalize current among devices connected in parallel.

datasheet-031.question: Which is correct about a MOSFET with VGS(th) specified as 1.0–2.5 V (ID = 250 µA)?
choices: As long as VGS is at or above the maximum VGS(th) of 2.5 V, the RDS(on) specified in the table is obtained
VGS(th) rises with temperature, so the MOSFET becomes harder to turn on at higher temperatures
VGS(th) is the voltage at which a tiny current begins to flow; low RDS(on) requires driving at the specified VGS
datasheet-031.explanation: VGS(th) is the gate voltage at which the drain current reaches a tiny value such as 250 µA; at this point, large currents still cannot flow with low resistance. RDS(on) is specified with conditions such as VGS = 10 V or 4.5 V, so check whether RDS(on) is specified at the voltage you can actually drive. To drive directly from a 3.3 V microcontroller, choose a logic-level part specified at VGS = 2.5 V or similar. VGS(th) decreases as temperature rises, so the device actually turns on more easily at high temperature.

datasheet-032.question: A MOSFET with total gate charge Qg = 50 nC is driven with a 10 V gate voltage at a switching frequency of 100 kHz. Roughly how much power is needed to drive the gate?
choices: 50 mW
5 mW
500 mW
datasheet-032.explanation: Qg is the charge needed to charge the gate once, and the drive power is P = Qg × VGS × f = 50 nC × 10 V × 100 kHz = 50 mW. The average gate current is Qg × f = 5 mA. This power is dissipated mainly in the driver IC and gate resistor. Because the gate input capacitance varies greatly with voltage (the Miller effect), Qg, which directly gives the charge required, is more convenient for drive-circuit design than a capacitance value. For example, driving at 1 A, the charging time can be estimated at about 50 ns.

datasheet-033.question: Which is the correct way to read a power MOSFET's safe operating area (SOA) graph?
choices: The DC line is outermost, and for pulsed operation, the shorter the pulse, the more strictly it is limited compared with DC
The boundary is set only by the absolute maximum ratings of VDS and ID, so it does not change with pulse width or case temperature
Shorter pulses allow higher power, and most graphs are for 25 °C single pulses, so derate according to temperature
datasheet-033.explanation: The SOA is a log-log graph with VDS on the horizontal axis and ID on the vertical axis, showing the combinations of voltage and current at which the device can be used without damage. The boundary is set by the RDS(on) limit, the current rating, the thermal (power) limit and so on; the thermal limit relaxes as pulse width shortens, so multiple lines such as 10 µs, 1 ms and DC are drawn. Most graphs are for a case temperature of 25 °C and a single pulse, so derate them for the actual temperature and repetitive operation. This is especially important when operating in the linear region, as in inrush-current limiting circuits.

datasheet-034.question: Which is correct about the reverse recovery time trr in a diode datasheet?
choices: It is a constant inherent to the device, so it has the same value under any circuit conditions
It varies with conditions such as forward current IF, the rate of current decrease di/dt and temperature, so read it together with the test conditions
Schottky barrier diodes generally have a longer trr than ordinary PN-junction diodes
datasheet-034.explanation: trr is the time during which reverse current flows, after switching from forward conduction to reverse bias, until the stored minority carriers are swept out. The amount of stored charge varies with forward current and temperature, and the waveform also changes with how fast the current is switched (di/dt), so datasheets specify it with conditions such as "IF = 1 A, di/dt = 100 A/µs." It is on the order of µs for general-purpose rectifiers and several tens of ns for fast-recovery types. Schottky diodes operate with majority carriers, so they have almost no reverse recovery.

datasheet-035.question: For an op-amp with a slew rate of 0.5 V/µs, roughly what is the maximum frequency at which a sine wave with an amplitude (peak) of 10 V can be output without distortion?
choices: About 8 kHz
About 50 kHz
About 800 Hz
datasheet-035.explanation: The maximum slope of a sine wave Vp sin(2πft) is 2πf × Vp. If this exceeds the slew rate, the output cannot keep up and distorts into a triangle-like wave. f = SR/(2π × Vp) = 0.5 × 10⁶ V/s ÷ (2π × 10 V) ≈ 8 kHz. This is called the full-power bandwidth, and it falls as amplitude increases. Note that even if the gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is sufficient, bandwidth for large-amplitude signals is limited by the slew rate. About 50 kHz is the value obtained by forgetting to multiply by 2π.

datasheet-036.question: A non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 100 is built using an op-amp with an input offset voltage of max 2 mV. With the input at 0 V, which is the guide for the maximum error voltage that can appear at the output?
choices: 2 mV
200 mV
20 mV
datasheet-036.explanation: Input offset voltage behaves like a small voltage source in series with the input and appears at the output multiplied by the non-inverting amplifier's gain (1 + Rf/Ri). 2 mV × 100 = 200 mV, which is a 4% error against a 5 V full scale, for example. Estimate with the max value rather than the typ value, and also add the change due to temperature drift (µV/°C). For precision measurement, choose a zero-drift (chopper) type with an offset of a few µV, or calibrate in software. 2 mV is the value obtained by forgetting to multiply by the gain.

datasheet-037.question: The datasheet of an op-amp used on a single 5 V supply gives the common-mode input range as "0 V to (V+ − 1.5 V)." Which is correct?
choices: 0–5 V is within the absolute maximum ratings, so even with a 4 V input, a voltage follower outputs correctly
It means the output voltage can swing only over 0–3.5 V; there is no limit on the input range
Correct operation is not guaranteed for inputs above 3.5 V, so a voltage follower cannot handle a 4 V signal
datasheet-037.explanation: The common-mode input range is the range within which the device amplifies as specified, provided the voltages on both input pins are within it. Here the upper limit is 5 − 1.5 = 3.5 V, so applying 4 V to a voltage follower, where the input voltage is directly the common-mode voltage, causes the output to distort or stick. Outside the range but within the absolute maximum ratings, the device will not be damaged, but operation is not guaranteed. The range over which the output can swing is specified separately as "output voltage swing," and devices usable close to both supply rails are called rail-to-rail.

datasheet-038.question: A 3.3 V output LDO has a dropout voltage specified as max 300 mV (at 500 mA output current). What is the minimum input voltage needed to maintain the output voltage while supplying 500 mA?
datasheet-038.explanation: Dropout voltage is the minimum voltage difference required between input and output to maintain the output voltage. Adding the max of 300 mV to the 3.3 V output, the input must be 3.6 V or higher. Dropout voltage increases with output current and, in many cases, at higher temperature, so use the value specified under the current and temperature conditions of your application. For example, if a lithium-ion battery's voltage falls to 3.5 V, the output can no longer hold 3.3 V and begins to drop. 3.0 V is the mistake of subtracting the dropout voltage instead of adding it.

datasheet-039.question: An LDO with a PSRR (power supply rejection ratio) of 60 dB at 1 kHz has a 1 kHz, 100 mV ripple on its input. Which is the guide for the ripple appearing at the output?
choices: 0.1 µV
About 1.7 mV
0.1 mV
datasheet-039.explanation: Voltage ratios in decibels use 20 log₁₀, so 60 dB is 1/1000. 100 mV ÷ 1000 = 0.1 mV appears at the output. 0.1 µV is the mistake of calculating with 10 log₁₀ (power ratio), and about 1.7 mV is the mistake of dividing 100 by 60. PSRR generally decreases at higher frequencies; even with 60 dB at 1 kHz, some products drop to around 20–30 dB at several hundred kHz. When placing an LDO after a switching regulator, check the PSRR at that switching frequency in the graph.

datasheet-040.question: Which condition is most closely related to the "no missing codes" guarantee in an A/D converter datasheet?
choices: Integral nonlinearity (INL) is within ±0.5 LSB
Differential nonlinearity (DNL) is greater than −1 LSB
Effective number of bits (ENOB) equals the resolution in bits
datasheet-040.explanation: DNL expresses how much the spacing between adjacent codes (code width) deviates from the ideal 1 LSB. When DNL reaches −1 LSB, that code's width becomes zero, producing a missing code that is never output no matter how the input is varied. Therefore, if DNL is greater than −1 LSB, no missing codes occur. Datasheets guarantee this together with the resolution, as in "12 bits, no missing codes." INL is the accumulated deviation from the ideal straight line and does not directly determine whether missing codes exist.

datasheet-041.question: A 16-bit A/D converter has a SINAD (signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio) of 74 dB. Roughly what is its effective number of bits (ENOB)?
choices: About 12 bits
16 bits
About 14 bits
datasheet-041.explanation: The SNR of an ideal N-bit ADC is determined only by quantization noise and is 6.02N + 1.76 dB. Using this in reverse gives ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02 = (74 − 1.76)/6.02 ≈ 12.0 bits. It means that, despite its 16-bit output, noise and distortion make its actual performance equivalent to an ideal 12-bit ADC. SINAD varies with input signal frequency and amplitude, so check the value or graph at a frequency close to your operating conditions. Resolution and actual accuracy are different things.

datasheet-042.question: Which is the common pin-numbering convention for packages such as QFP and SOP?
choices: Pin 1 is next to the index mark, and numbers increase clockwise when viewed from the top
Pin 1 is next to the index mark, and numbers increase counterclockwise when viewed from the top
With the package oriented so the marking is readable, pin 1 is at the bottom right and numbers increase to the left
datasheet-042.explanation: The top of the package has an index mark—a dimple, dot, notch or chamfer—and pin 1 is next to it. Pins 2, 3 and so on generally increase counterclockwise when viewed from the top. Always check whether the datasheet's pin diagram is a top view or a bottom view. In a bottom view, left and right appear reversed, and confusing the two leads to the mistake of a mirror-image footprint on the board. BGAs use numbers such as A1, with rows as letters and columns as numbers.

datasheet-043.question: Which is the common way to handle the large exposed pad on the bottom of a QFN package?
choices: Soldering it makes it prone to cracking from thermal stress, so provide no land on the board and leave it floating above the board
To keep it electrically isolated, cover the corresponding area of the board with solder resist and do not connect it
Provide a land on the board, solder the pad, connect it to the specified potential (often GND) and conduct heat away through thermal vias
datasheet-043.explanation: The exposed pad is the underside of the die pad, on which the chip is mounted, exposed outside the package; it is the main path for heat into the board. The datasheet θJA value is typically measured with this pad soldered to the board and connected to inner-layer planes through thermal vias, and leaving it unsoldered greatly degrades heat dissipation. The recommended land pattern may also show the stencil aperture divided into segments to adjust the solder volume and prevent voids and component lifting. Follow the datasheet for the potential to connect it to.

datasheet-044.question: A datasheet states "ESD rating: HBM ±2 kV, CDM ±500 V." Which is the correct interpretation of these values?
choices: They are component-level ratings assuming handling of the part, not ratings for ESD applied to external terminals of the finished equipment
The part withstands ESD up to ±2 kV, so no added protection components are needed even if it is connected directly to the equipment's external connector
HBM and CDM are different names for the same test, and CDM, with the smaller value, correctly represents the part's actual robustness
datasheet-044.explanation: HBM (human body model) simulates a discharge when a charged person touches a pin, and CDM (charged device model) simulates a discharge when a pin of a charged part touches metal; both are component-level ratings assuming handling in an ESD-controlled factory. Connectors and other parts of finished equipment are subject to far greater energy, such as ±8 kV contact discharge in system-level tests like IEC 61000-4-2. Pins brought out to the outside should, as a rule, be given separate protection components such as TVS diodes.

datasheet-045.question: Which is the correct handling of a surface-mount part marked MSL 3 (moisture sensitivity level 3)?
choices: After opening, reflow within 168 hours at 30 °C/60%RH or less; if exceeded, bake before mounting
The number 3 means the number of times reflow soldering may be performed is limited to a maximum of three
It is a part little affected by moisture absorption, so after the moisture barrier bag is opened it can be stored and mounted without regard to time limits
datasheet-045.explanation: MSL is a moisture sensitivity classification defined in a JEDEC standard (J-STD-020) that indicates the time allowed between opening the moisture barrier bag and reflow (floor life). For MSL 3, it is 168 hours (one week) at 30 °C/60%RH or less. If a part is heated in reflow after absorbing moisture, the internal moisture vaporizes suddenly and the package can crack or delaminate (the popcorn effect), so parts past their limit are dried by baking at 125 °C or similar. Only MSL 1 can be handled without a time limit, and higher numbers require stricter control.

datasheet-046.question: Which correctly describes what "RoHS compliant" means for electronic components?
choices: A third-party certification body individually certifies each product as able to withstand the high reflow temperatures of lead-free solder
The amount of greenhouse gases emitted in the manufacturing process is kept below limits set by the EU
The content of specific hazardous substances defined by EU rules, such as lead, mercury, cadmium and hexavalent chromium, is below the limits
datasheet-046.explanation: RoHS is an EU rule restricting the use of specific hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment. It covers a total of 10 substances—lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, two brominated flame retardants (PBB and PBDE) and four phthalates—with limits of 0.1% by weight (0.01% for cadmium) per homogeneous material. Because RoHS-compliant parts presume mounting with lead-free solder, their tolerance of reflow conditions with a peak temperature of around 260 °C is often stated as well, but this is not a requirement of RoHS itself.

datasheet-047.question: What is the main purpose of checking a datasheet's revision history?
choices: To check shipment inspection results for each production lot and trends in the product's field failure rate
To understand specified values and content that have changed from previous versions and confirm that the document at hand is the latest
To check when and how the product's price and lead time have changed
datasheet-047.explanation: Datasheets are revised after publication, with changes to specified values, corrections of errors, revised pin function descriptions, added packages and so on. The revision history summarizes the changes in each version, so you can check the differences between the version used for design and the latest one. To avoid having designed based on max values from an old version, record the version referenced at design time. Changes to the specifications or manufacturing process of products in mass production are generally communicated to customers separately through a product change notification (PCN).

datasheet-048.question: Which correctly describes the content of a document called "errata" provided for microcontrollers and similar devices?
choices: A collection of only typos and omissions in the datasheet, unrelated to the product's operation
Known defects where the device does not operate as specified in the datasheet, along with the conditions under which they occur and workarounds
New features to be added to the product in the future and the planned availability date for each
datasheet-048.explanation: In complex ICs, behavior that differs from the specification is sometimes discovered after shipment. Errata are documents that compile such known defects together with the affected chip revisions, the conditions under which they occur and workarounds (software fixes, usage restrictions, etc.). For example: "Under certain conditions a peripheral flag may not be set, so check the status by another method." Corrections of documentation errors may also be included, but the main purpose is to report defects in actual operation, and errata must always be checked early in design.

datasheet-049.question: Which is the correct way to treat the "Typical Characteristics" graphs in a datasheet?
choices: They show trends of representative samples and are not guaranteed values; design should be based on the min/max in the tables
Even values for conditions not given in the tables can be used directly as guaranteed values, as long as they are read from the graphs
They show results calculated by simulation, so they have no relation to measured values of actual products
datasheet-049.explanation: Typical characteristics graphs show, as measured on representative samples, how characteristics change as temperature, supply voltage, load, frequency and so on are varied. Many graphs are annotated "typ" or "typical," and the spread is not shown. Base designs on the min/max in the tables, and use the graphs to understand trends with conditions or to get a rough idea of values under conditions not in the tables. For example, you might estimate a high-temperature value by correcting the 25 °C max value using the rate of change with temperature read from a graph.

datasheet-050.question: On a graph with a logarithmic horizontal axis, which value is closest to the one represented by the position exactly midway between the 10 and 100 tick marks?
choices: About 32
datasheet-050.explanation: On a logarithmic scale, position is proportional to the logarithm of the value. The midpoint between log₁₀10 = 1 and log₁₀100 = 2 is 1.5, so the value is 10 to the power 1.5, i.e. √1000 ≈ 31.6. Similarly, within one decade, 2 lies at about 30% and 5 at about 70% of the width. Many datasheet graphs, such as frequency responses and SOA, have logarithmic axes; the tick spacing is not uniform, so reading them with a linear intuition leads to large misreadings. 55 is the arithmetic mean of 10 and 100, the midpoint on a linear scale.
